extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and practitioners) performing 35 U.S.C. §101 subject-matter eligibility analyses for nature-based product claims
extracted.subtask_description: A stepwise worksheet for analyzing whether patent claims to nature-based products satisfy 35 U.S.C. §101, following the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance and July 2015 Update; includes claim construction, Step 1 statutory category, Step 2A judicial-exception/markedly-different analysis, and Step 2B 'significantly more' inventive-concept evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify what applicant invented and claim construction (BRI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review the disclosure to identify what applicant considers as the invention (MPEP 2103(I)). Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim based on plain meaning and specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This can be a brief description and should not merely reproduce the claim. The take away is what the invention is focused on (e.g., 'vaccine'). Establish BRI showing how terms are interpreted (example: BRI of 'inactivated Pigeon flu virus' = dead virus chemically modified by formalin so nucleic acids are chemically modified and cannot reproduce, in an amount to produce an immunogenic response). Use a separate worksheet for each claim; use Quick Reference Sheet/flowchart/form paragraphs as aids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — Statutory category determination (process/machine/manufacture/composition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claimed invention falls within one of the four statutory categories of invention (process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose A (yes) to continue with the SME analysis. If B (no), make a rejection as drawn to non-statutory subject matter using Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01 available in Custom OACs. If claim could be amended to fall within a statutory category, it is recommended to continue the SME analysis under that assumption and document the assumption clearly in the record; if no amendment is possible, end SME analysis and continue with examination of other patentability requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A — Identify whether claim is directed to a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide if the claim is directed to a product of nature, law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea (judicially recognized exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim is 'directed' to a product of nature exception when it recites a nature-based product limitation that does not exhibit markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state. For other exceptions, identify if the claimed concept aligns with judicial exceptions (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas). Use case law chart and Interim Eligibility Guidance for assistance. Choose: A (not directed to exception) — conclude SME and continue examination; B (streamlined analysis appropriate) — conclude SME if eligibility is self-evident; C (directed to exception) — proceed to detailed analysis (identify limitations and compare to natural counterparts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics analysis for nature-based products
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim recites a nature-based product limitation, compare the claimed nature-based product to its closest naturally occurring counterpart to determine whether it exhibits 'markedly different characteristics' (if it does, it is not a product-of-nature exception).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete (a) identify the limitation(s) that set forth the nature-based product; (b) identify the closest naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state; (c) compare claimed product to counterpart and choose (i) exhibits markedly different characteristics or (ii) lacks markedly different characteristics. Non-limiting examples of characteristics considered include: biological or pharmacological functions or activities; chemical and physical properties; phenotype (functional and structural characteristics); and structure and form (chemical, genetic or physical). Example: inactivated virus chemically modified so it cannot replicate = marked difference (structure change and inability to replicate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Process claims exception nuance
rubrics_metrics.description: Note that process claims are generally not subject to the markedly different characteristics analysis for nature-based products used in the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception when process claim is drafted so there is no difference in substance from a product claim (e.g., 'a method of providing an apple.'). In such limited cases, treat process claim similar to product claim for the markedly-different analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis option
rubrics_metrics.description: If eligibility is self-evident and the claimed invention is not focused on an exception or does not attempt to tie up the exception, a streamlined SME analysis may be appropriate and a full eligibility analysis is not needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to training slides for examples. If using streamlined analysis, conclude SME and continue with examination of other patentability requirements. Document that streamlined analysis was used and why (e.g., claim clearly not directed to an exception).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify limitations reciting other exceptions (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim is directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon, identify which limitation(s) recite the exception and explain why they are considered a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the limitation(s) text and reasons why these are judicial exceptions (e.g., mathematical relationship, fundamental economic practice, naturally occurring principle), with supporting references to case law/chart. If no judicial exception found, conclude SME and continue with other examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — Identify additional elements beyond the exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim recites any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) beyond the exception(s) identified, including combinations of naturally occurring components that do not occur together in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no additional elements exist, conclude SME analysis with a §101 rejection (use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015) and consider whether disclosure contains elements that could be added to make claim eligible (identify suggested elements). If other elements are present, list them and continue to evaluate their significance for constituting 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate significance of additional elements (search for 'inventive concept')
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the additional elements, individually or in combination, result in the claim as a whole amounting to 'significantly more' than the judicial exception (i.e., provide an inventive concept).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the invention identified in Section I and how additional elements relate to it. The additional elements must show an 'inventive concept.' Reasons supporting significance can include one or more of the following (each is a potential basis): improves another technology or technical field; improves the functioning of a computer itself; applies the exception with, or by use of, a particular machine (not a generic computer performing generic computer functions; not mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer; not adding words like 'apply it'); effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; adds a specific limitation other than what is well-understood, routine and conventional in the field (not appending routine activities at a high level of generality); adds unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application (not insignificant extrasolution activity such as mere data gathering); adds meaningful limitations that amount to more than generally linking the use of the exception to a particular technological environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-patterns and cautions when evaluating additional elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements that are generic, well-understood, routine, conventional, or high-level do not typically supply 'significantly more.' Generic computer implementation and mere instructions to 'apply' an exception are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat a generic computer performing generic computer functions as adding significantly more. Do not treat adding words equivalent to 'apply the exception' as sufficient. Do not treat appending well-understood routine and conventional activities, specified at a high level of generality, as providing an inventive concept. Mere data gathering or insignificant extrasolution activity is not enough. Use comparable case law examples (e.g., Funk Brothers) when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining component elements that do not occur together in nature
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claimed product comprises a combination of component elements that do not occur together in nature, treat each component element as an additional element to the other components for determining whether their combination results in significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the combination changes functional properties or structure in a marked way compared to individual natural components (example: peptide + aluminum adjuvant showing synergistic increased immunogenicity = markedly different characteristics; peptide + water mixture that leaves both components unchanged = not markedly different). Assess both individual contributions and their combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome decisions and required actions (eligible vs. §101 rejection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclude SME analysis based on the markedly-different and inventive-concept evaluations: If claim is not directed to any judicial exception or additional elements supply significantly more, conclude SME and continue examination of other patentability requirements; if not, make a §101 rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If making a §101 rejection, use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015 (or 7.05 and 7.05.01 for Step 1 non-statutory rejections) in Custom OACs. Identify the exception(s) the claim is directed to, explain why the claim lacks additional elements sufficient to amount to significantly more, and optionally suggest claim amendments or disclosure elements that could render the claim eligible (provide examples from the disclosure). The worksheet includes sample rejection language to populate Office Actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of supporting materials and examples (case law and training materials)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance, July 2015 Update, Quick Reference Sheets, the Subject Matter Eligibility Court Decisions chart, case law examples (e.g., Chakrabarty, Myriad, Funk Brothers), and training slides to inform the analysis and identify judicial exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The worksheet suggests cross-referencing the Quick Reference Sheet (flowchart and form paragraphs), the July 2015 Update chart of abstract idea concepts, and the court decisions chart. Use example analyses (several Example 28 claims provided) to guide application of the markedly-different and significantly-more analyses and to craft Office Action language or amendment suggestions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation and remediation suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Where appropriate, document interpretations and suggested claim amendments or disclosure elements in the record to clarify conclusions or offer applicant paths to eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If assuming an amendment to reach a statutory category, make the assumption clear in the record. When finding ineligibility, identify elements in the disclosure that could be added to claims to make them eligible (examples given: immuno-effective amount of an aluminum salt adjuvant). Provide suggested form-paragraph language and sample rejection text to populate Office Actions.
